intro: The fast movement of Bartók’s Second Quartet sets repeated notes against shifting accents. Its narrow melodic figures owe something to the Arab music he recorded in Algeria, rather than to a Hungarian dance tune.
question: How can one repeated note drive a whole movement?

cues.title: A pitch that stays put
cues.text: Through the opening stretch, listen for repeated notes beneath the moving lines. A fixed pitch can provide an anchor without supplying a new chord on every beat; changing accents keep repetition from becoming a regular tread.
cues.evidence: Roger Parker’s Gresham lecture describes the opening repeated-note accompaniment. The analysis finds densely packed attacks through the first minute; this is a passage-level listening guide. https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An anchor, not a key
cues.text: A repeated pitch does not necessarily establish a major or minor key. Follow the notes that stay put against the moving parts; the clashes need not mean that the music has changed its tonal centre.
cues.evidence: Parker distinguishes Bartók’s repeated-note centres from conventional key progressions. The recording’s fluctuating key estimates cannot resolve that distinction. https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Beyond Hungarian folk song
cues.text: Bartók’s collecting took him as far as Biskra in Algeria. Roger Parker connects this movement’s narrow melodies, ornaments and repeated rhythms with that North African fieldwork, rather than treating it as an arrangement of a Hungarian dance.
cues.evidence: Roger Parker discusses the Algerian fieldwork and its relationship to this movement in his 2007 Gresham lecture. https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

cues.title: The attacks gather again
cues.text: Across this stretch, the attacks become more closely packed after a less active passage. Compare the spacing of the notes with the weight of the sound: the two can increase together without being the same musical change.
cues.evidence: The analysis detects more attacks from about 1:45 to 1:55 than around 1:30–1:40, alongside a rising relative level within this recording.

cues.title: The drive breaks apart
cues.text: In this stretch, the forceful texture gives way to quieter, more separated gestures. Listen for the difference between a pause inside a phrase and a longer interruption of the repeated-note drive.
cues.evidence: Several detected changes cluster around 2:18–2:34. Relative level falls substantially between 2:15 and 2:45; the report does not identify individual instrumental gestures.

cues.title: Space between the attacks
cues.text: Through the quieter middle passages, follow the space between attacks rather than trying to maintain the opening’s continuous pulse. A sustained note and a repeated note organise time differently even when both hold the same pitch.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a low-level stretch around 3:30–3:45, with fewer detected attacks than in the opening. Their individual pitches and players are not established by this measurement.

cues.title: Between two slower movements
cues.text: The quartet was written during the First World War. Its three movements place this Allegro between a Moderato and a Lento: the rapid dance is the centre of the work, not its final destination.
cues.evidence: Parker’s Gresham lecture documents the wartime composition and the three-movement order. https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

cues.title: Colour without more attacks
cues.text: Through this passage, compare the edge of the string sound with the spacing of its attacks. A more penetrating colour need not mean faster notes; sustained sound can carry intensity too.
cues.evidence: The report shows increasing high-frequency weight around 4:40–5:05 while detected attacks become less frequent. This measurement does not identify a bowing technique or player.

cues.title: Dense attacks return
cues.text: Around this stretch, closely packed attacks restore the earlier sense of drive. Listen for the change in articulation as well as the increase in force: sustained sound and repeated sound can occupy the same register very differently.
cues.evidence: A detected change near 5:20 accompanies a large rise in attack density compared with 4:55–5:05. It supports a textural contrast, not a precisely aligned thematic return.

cues.title: Pressure, then withdrawal
cues.text: Across this stretch, a forceful crest gives way to a prolonged withdrawal. Follow the reduction in weight without assuming that quieter music must also be slower.
cues.evidence: Relative level peaks around 5:55, then falls substantially through 6:10–6:25. The five-second measurements support the broad contour, not a beat-level boundary.

cues.title: Speed without a loud climax
cues.text: Bartók marks the closing Prestissimo pianissimo and asks for mutes. Listen through the final section for the separation between speed and force: the fastest writing need not be the strongest-sounding.
cues.evidence: Parker describes the muted, quiet Prestissimo. Its approximate placement follows the score’s closing position and the recording’s withdrawal around 6:10–6:30; it has not been checked by ear. https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A final burst
cues.text: The closing stretch contrasts a renewed burst of sound with a rapid decay. Within the complete quartet, this movement’s ending is followed by a Lento rather than another fast conclusion.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 7:10–7:20, then falls sharply by 7:25–7:30. The following Lento is documented in Parker’s account of the quartet.

transitions.title: The repeated-note engine breaks apart
transitions.how: Bartók loosens the dance by interrupting its repeated attacks, not by steering a dominant chord into a new tonic. The opening’s D-centred ostinato has made a pitch function like a drum; now separated gestures and longer notes weaken that continuous reference. Across the contrasting episodes the quartet can spread into a high violin line above plucked cello rather than four parts caught in the same rhythmic pressure. Narrow intervals and ornaments remain part of the language, but the gaps between them become structural.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Contrasting episodes, 142 s. The report clusters changes at 2:18–2:34 and shows relative level falling through 2:45. Roger Parker describes the score’s repeated D, non-functional pitch centres and contrasting high-violin/pizzicato-cello episode; that scoring describes the ensuing span, not an entrance at 142 s. https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

transitions.title: Short attacks reclaim the pulse
transitions.how: The more sustained writing gives way to tightly repeated, accented string attacks. Bartók recovers the dance through its behaviour: a fixed-note insistence under narrow, turning melodic figures, with accents that resist a comfortable tread. The bass participates in that rhythmic pressure rather than preparing a conventional dominant–tonic cadence. Repetition rebuilds the sense of a centre, but does not make this a return to D major or D minor in the classical sense. The ostinato’s renewed grip matters more than a copied melody.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Dense attacks return, 320 s. The report marks 5:20 and rises from 0.2–0.6 detected attacks/s around 4:55–5:05 to 6.2 at 5:20. Parker describes the repeated-rhythm returns in the score. The relations file explicitly declines a literal-repeat arc; neither the key estimates nor the attack detector identifies a precise returning bar. https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

transitions.title: Faster, muted, almost weightless
transitions.how: The preceding force drains away before the closing Prestissimo. Bartók separates speed from weight: the quartet puts on mutes and plays pianissimo while the small repeated-note and turning figures rush past faster. The reduction in resonance changes the sound of all four instruments without adding or removing a player. This is a compression of the dance’s rhythmic vocabulary, not a new lyrical theme or a reassuring modulation into a major key. Listen for the quick motion continuing after the emphatic attack has been withdrawn.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Closing rush, 388 s. The report’s strongest boundary is 6:28; relative level has fallen from −8.6 dB at 5:55 to −32.3 dB at 6:25, with lower brightness thereafter. Parker documents the score’s muted, pianissimo Prestissimo. This approximate anchor does not claim that the onset detector measures its actual speed. https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

Piano professor, Budapest Academy, 1907–34 · Hungarian Academy of Sciences folk-music project, 1934–40 · Columbia University research in American exile

Six string quartets · three piano concertos · two violin concertos · three stage works · folk-music collections and pedagogical music
composer.background:
Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós, a town in the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary which became part of Romania after the First World War. His father, who directed an agricultural school, died in 1888; his mother, Paula Voit, supported Béla and his sister by teaching. After several moves the family settled in Pozsony, now Bratislava. The changing names on this map matter: the Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian communities he later recorded occupied overlapping musical territories. His professional education began within the German-speaking conservatoire tradition.

At the Budapest Academy from 1899 to 1903, he studied piano with István Thomán, a pupil of Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler. Hearing Richard Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra in 1902 helped release him from student exercises. Kossuth, composed in 1903, made the Hungarian revolutionary leader the subject of a large orchestral narrative and caricatured Haydn’s imperial anthem as the Austrian enemy. This early nationalist programme preceded the comparative research that would complicate his understanding of national music.
composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: A pianist and fieldworker who turned the modes, rhythms and performance habits of peasant music into new kinds of quartet and orchestral argument.
